p.src: Meanwhile, as Sun Quan was marshaling his forces at Ruxu, a sudden report came that Cao Cao was leading four hundred thousand troops from Hanzhong to relieve Hefei. Sun Quan consulted his advisers, then first detached Dong Xi and Xu Sheng with fifty large ships to lie in ambush at Ruxu; and ordered Chen Wu to lead a force in patrolling the riverbanks. Zhang Zhao said, “Cao Cao has come from afar; we must first blunt the enemy’s ardor.” Sun Quan therefore asked those beneath his command, “Cao Cao has come from afar. Who dares strike first and defeat the enemy, thereby blunting his ardor?” Ling Tong stepped forward and said, “I am willing to go.” Sun Quan asked, “How many troops will you take?” Ling Tong replied, “Three thousand will suffice.” Gan Ning said, “A mere hundred horsemen would be enough to defeat the enemy. What need is there for three thousand?” Ling Tong flew into a rage. The two began contending with each other before Sun Quan. Sun Quan said, “Cao Cao’s army is formidable; the enemy must not be taken lightly.” He then ordered Ling Tong to take three thousand troops out from Ruxu to reconnoiter and to engage any of Cao Cao’s soldiers he encountered.

p.src: Ling Tong accepted the order and led three thousand troops out from the Ruxu stockade. Where clouds of dust arose, Cao Cao’s troops had already arrived. The vanguard commander Zhang Liao engaged Ling Tong, and after fifty bouts neither had gained the advantage. Fearing that Ling Tong might come to harm, Sun Quan ordered Lü Meng to support him and bring him back to camp. When Gan Ning saw Ling Tong return, he told Sun Quan, “Tonight I shall take only one hundred men to raid Cao Cao’s camp; if I lose so much as one man or one horse, it shall not count as a feat.” Sun Quan admired his courage. He assigned him one hundred picked cavalrymen from his own command and bestowed fifty jars of wine and fifty jin of mutton upon the soldiers. Gan Ning returned to his encampment. He had all one hundred men sit in rows, then filled a silver bowl with wine and himself drank two bowls first. Then he addressed them: “Tonight we are under orders to raid the enemy camp. I ask each of you to drain a full cup and strive valiantly forward.” At these words, the men looked uneasily at one another. Seeing their troubled expressions, Gan Ning drew his sword and angrily rebuked them: “I am a senior commander, yet even I do not begrudge my life; how dare you hesitate!” Seeing Gan Ning’s anger, they all rose and bowed, saying, “We are ready to fight to the death.”

p.src: Gan Ning shared the wine and meat with the hundred men. When they had finished, and the second watch drew near, he took one hundred white goose feathers and had each man fix one to his helmet as an identifying mark; then all donned armor, mounted their horses, and sped to the edge of Cao Cao’s camp. Tearing aside the abatis, they gave a great shout and charged inside, making straight for the central camp to kill Cao Cao. But the troops of the central camp had barricaded the approaches with carts and weapons, linked together in an enclosure as tight as an iron barrel, so they could advance no farther. With only his hundred horsemen, Gan Ning charged left and right. Cao Cao’s soldiers panicked, and having no notion how many enemies there were, fell into confusion among themselves. Gan Ning’s hundred riders galloped unchecked throughout the camp, killing whomever they encountered. Every camp erupted in clamor; torches rose like stars, and the shouting shook the heavens. Gan Ning fought his way out through the camp’s southern gate, and none dared stand against him. Sun Quan ordered Zhou Tai to bring a detachment to his support. Gan Ning brought his hundred riders safely back to Ruxu. Fearing an ambush, Cao Cao’s troops did not dare pursue them. A later poet composed these lines in praise:

p.src: Gan Ning led his hundred riders back to camp without losing a single man or horse; on reaching the camp gate, he ordered all one hundred men to beat drums and play flutes while crying, “Long live our lord!” Their jubilant cries rang out thunderously. Sun Quan came in person to welcome them. Gan Ning dismounted and bowed to the ground. Sun Quan raised him, took his hand, and said, “Your expedition, General, was enough to strike terror into that old villain. It was not that I wished to cast you away; I merely wished to witness your courage.” He immediately awarded him one thousand bolts of silk and one hundred keen blades. After bowing and accepting the gifts, Gan Ning distributed them among his hundred men. Sun Quan told his commanders, “Mengde has Zhang Liao, and I have Gan Xingba; they are well matched.”

p.src: The next day, Zhang Liao led out troops to challenge them to battle. Seeing that Gan Ning had won distinction, Ling Tong declared fervently, “I wish to face Zhang Liao.” Sun Quan gave his consent. Ling Tong then led five thousand troops out from Ruxu. Sun Quan personally brought Gan Ning to the battlefront to watch the fight. When the opposing formations had been drawn up, Zhang Liao rode forth, with Li Dian on his left and Yue Jin on his right. Ling Tong spurred his horse, raised his saber, and rode before the battle line. Zhang Liao sent Yue Jin out to meet him. The two fought for fifty bouts without either gaining victory. When Cao Cao heard of it, he personally rode beneath the gate banner to watch. Seeing the two commanders locked in fierce combat, he ordered Cao Xiu to loose a treacherous arrow from concealment. Cao Xiu slipped behind Zhang Liao, drew his bow, and shot an arrow that struck Ling Tong’s mount squarely. The horse reared upright and threw Ling Tong to the ground. Yue Jin hurriedly thrust his spear at him. Before the spear could reach him, a bowstring twanged, and an arrow struck Yue Jin full in the face, sending him tumbling from his horse. Both armies rushed forward, each rescuing its own commander and carrying him back to camp; the gongs sounded to end the battle. On returning to camp, Ling Tong bowed in gratitude to Sun Quan. Sun Quan said, “The man who shot the arrow and saved you was Gan Ning.” Ling Tong then knocked his head upon the ground before Gan Ning and said, “I never imagined that you would show me such great kindness!” From that time onward, he and Gan Ning became friends pledged to life and death, and he never again bore him ill will.

p.src: Meanwhile, when Cao Cao saw that Yue Jin had been struck by an arrow, he personally returned to the command tent to tend his wound. The next day, he divided his army into five columns to attack Ruxu: Cao Cao himself commanded the center; on the left, the first column was led by Zhang Liao and the second by Li Dian; on the right, the first column was led by Xu Huang and the second by Pang De. Each column had ten thousand troops and charged toward the riverbank. At the time, the two commanders Dong Xi and Xu Sheng were aboard their ships; when the five columns approached, fear showed on the faces of all their troops. Xu Sheng said, “We receive our lord’s stipend and must serve him loyally. What is there to fear?” He then led several hundred valiant men across the river in small boats and charged into Li Dian’s army. Aboard his ship, Dong Xi ordered the troops to beat the drums and shout encouragement. Suddenly, a violent wind arose over the river; white-crested waves surged toward the sky, and the waters seethed tumultuously. Seeing that the great ship was about to capsize, the soldiers vied with one another to escape into the smaller boats. Sword in hand, Dong Xi cried out, “A commander has received his lord’s order to defend this place against the enemy. How dare you abandon ship and flee?” He immediately beheaded more than ten men who had left the ship. Before long, the gale intensified and the ship overturned; Dong Xi ultimately perished in the waters at the river mouth. Within Li Dian’s army, Xu Sheng charged back and forth.

Zhou Tai said, “My lord, follow me and fight your way out.” Zhou Tai went in front and Sun Quan behind, and together they charged forward with all their strength. Sun Quan said, “Arrows and bolts are raining down together; I cannot get out. What are we to do?” Zhou Tai replied, “My lord, go in front and let me follow behind. p.src: Sun Quan spurred his horse forward. Zhou Tai shielded him on every side. Though struck by several spears and pierced through his layered armor by arrows, he brought Sun Quan to safety. When they reached the riverbank, Lü Meng came with a naval force to meet them and take them aboard. Sun Quan said, “But for Zhou Tai charging through the enemy three times, I could never have escaped that close encirclement. Yet Xu Sheng is still trapped at its heart. How can he escape?” Zhou Tai said, “I shall go back and save him.” Brandishing his spear, he wheeled around and fought his way back into the encirclement, rescuing Xu Sheng. Both generals were gravely wounded. Lü Meng ordered his soldiers to hold the troops on the bank at bay with a storm of arrows and brought the two generals aboard.

p.src: Meanwhile, Chen Wu was locked in fierce combat with Pang De. With no reinforcements behind him, Pang De drove him to the mouth of a valley thick with trees. When Chen Wu tried to turn and fight again, a tree caught his sleeve. Unable to meet the attack, he was slain by Pang De. Seeing that Sun Quan had escaped, Cao Cao personally urged on his horse and troops, pursued them to the river, and exchanged volleys with them. Lü Meng ran out of arrows. Just as he was in distress, a fleet suddenly approached from across the river. At its head was the great general Lu Xun, Sun Ce’s son-in-law, who had personally brought a hundred thousand troops. A volley drove Cao Cao’s troops back. Pressing their advantage, Lu Xun’s men landed, pursued and slaughtered them, and recaptured several thousand warhorses. Countless soldiers of Cao Cao’s army were wounded, and the force returned in crushing defeat. Amid the confusion of battle, Chen Wu’s body was found.

p.src: When Sun Quan learned that Chen Wu had fallen and Dong Xi had drowned in the river, his grief was profound. He ordered men into the water to recover Dong Xi’s body and gave it a lavish burial together with Chen Wu’s. Grateful also for Zhou Tai’s service in protecting and rescuing him, Sun Quan held a banquet in his honor. Sun Quan personally filled his cup, stroked his back, and said with tears streaming down his face, “Twice you saved me, sparing no thought for your own life. You suffered scores of spear wounds, and your skin is carved all over with scars. How could I fail to treat you with the affection due my own flesh and blood, or entrust you with the grave command of troops? You are my meritorious officer; I shall share honor and disgrace, joy and sorrow with you.” When he had finished, he ordered Zhou Tai to remove his clothes and show the assembled generals. His flesh and skin looked as though gouged by knives, with knotted scars covering his whole body. Sun Quan pointed to each scar in turn and asked how he had received it. Zhou Tai recounted in detail how each wound had been suffered in battle. For every wound, Sun Quan made him drink a goblet of wine. That day Zhou Tai became very drunk. Sun Quan bestowed on him a green silk parasol and ordered that it be carried over him whenever he came or went, as a mark of distinction.

p.src: At Ruxu, Sun Quan opposed Cao Cao for more than a month without gaining victory. Zhang Zhao and Gu Yong advised him, “Cao Cao’s power is great and cannot be overcome by force. If we wage a protracted war against him, our soldiers will suffer grievous losses. It would be best to seek peace and bring security to the people.” Sun Quan accepted their counsel and sent Bu Zhi to Cao Cao’s camp to seek peace, promising to present annual tribute. Seeing that the lands south of the Yangtze could not soon be conquered, Cao Cao agreed, declaring, “Sun Quan must withdraw his men and horses first; then I shall return with my army.” Bu Zhi returned with the reply. Sun Quan left only Jiang Qin and Zhou Tai to guard the mouth of Ruxu, embarked the rest of his great army, and returned to Moling.

p.src: Cao Cao left Cao Ren and Zhang Liao to garrison Hefei, then returned with his army to Xuchang. The civil and military officials all proposed that Cao Cao be made King of Wei. Cui Yan, Minister of State, vehemently declared that this must not be done. The other officials said, “Have you alone not seen what happened to Xun Wenruo?” Cui Yan cried angrily, “The times! The times! Change must surely come! Let him do as he pleases!” Someone who was at odds with Cui Yan reported his words to Cao Cao. Cao Cao flew into a rage, had Cui Yan arrested and imprisoned, and put him to examination. With his tiger-like eyes and curling beard, Cui Yan did nothing but revile Cao Cao as a treacherous villain who deceived his sovereign. p.src: In the fifth month of summer, the twenty-first year of Jian’an, the ministers submitted a memorial to Emperor Xian extolling the achievements and virtue of Cao Cao, Duke of Wei, as reaching heaven and spanning earth, beyond even Yi Yin and the Duke of Zhou, and declaring that he should be elevated to the rank of king. Emperor Xian at once ordered Zhong Yao to draft an edict investing Cao Cao as King of Wei. Cao Cao made a show of submitting three memorials of refusal. Three times the edict replied that his refusal would not be accepted. Cao Cao then bowed to the command and accepted the title of King of Wei. He wore a crown with twelve pendants, rode in a golden-root carriage drawn by six horses, employed the sovereign’s carriages, robes, bells, and ceremonial regalia, and had the roads cleared at his departure and barred at his entrance. He built a palace for the King of Wei in Ye Commandery and deliberated over appointing an heir apparent. Cao Cao’s principal wife, Lady Ding, had borne no children. His concubine Lady Liu had borne a son, Cao Ang, who died at Wancheng during the campaign against Zhang Xiu. Lady Bian had borne four sons: the eldest was Pi, the second Zhang, the third Zhi, and the fourth Xiong. Cao Cao therefore set Lady Ding aside and made Lady Bian consort of the King of Wei.

Lady Bian had borne four sons: the eldest was Pi, the second Zhang, the third Zhi, and the fourth Xiong.
Cao Cao therefore set Lady Ding aside and made Lady Bian consort of the King of Wei.

p.src: The third son, Cao Zhi, styled Zijian, was exceptionally intelligent and could produce a finished composition the moment he took up his brush. Cao Cao wished to make him his heir. The eldest son, Cao Pi, fearing that he would not be chosen, asked Palace Counsellor Jia Xu for advice. Jia Xu instructed him what to do. Thereafter, whenever Cao Cao went on campaign and his sons saw him off, Cao Zhi would recite his father’s achievements and virtues, shaping every utterance into an elegant composition. Cao Pi alone, when bidding farewell to his father, merely wept and bowed, moving all those around him. Cao Cao then began to suspect Cao Zhi of artifice, judging his sincerity inferior to Cao Pi’s. Cao Pi also sent men to bribe Cao Cao’s attendants, who all spoke highly of his virtue. When Cao Cao wished to appoint an heir, he remained undecided and asked Jia Xu, “I wish to appoint my successor. Whom should I choose?” Jia Xu did not answer, and Cao Cao asked him why. Jia Xu said, “I was pondering something, and therefore could not answer at once.” Cao Cao asked, “What were you pondering?” Jia Xu replied, “I was thinking of Yuan Benchu and Liu Jingsheng and their sons.” Cao Cao laughed heartily and forthwith appointed his eldest son, Cao Pi, heir apparent to the king.

p.src: In the tenth month of winter, the palace of the King of Wei was completed. Agents were sent throughout the land to gather rare flowers and unusual fruits for planting in the rear garden. One envoy came to the land of Wu, met Sun Quan, delivered the King of Wei’s command, and then proceeded to Wenzhou to obtain mandarins. At the time Sun Quan was showing deference to the King of Wei, so he had more than forty loads of large mandarins selected in the city and sent by forced marches to Ye Commandery. Midway there, the burden-bearers grew exhausted and rested at the foot of a mountain. They saw a gentleman approach, blind in one eye and lame in one leg, wearing a white rattan cap and a loose blue robe. He saluted the porters and said, “You have labored hard beneath your loads. How would it be if this poor Daoist carried one stage of each for you?” The men were delighted. The gentleman then carried each load for five li. Every load he had carried became lighter. They were all astonished and suspicious. Before departing, the gentleman told the officer in charge of the mandarins, “This poor Daoist is an old acquaintance of the King of Wei from his native district. My surname is Zuo, my given name Ci, my style Yuanfang, and my Daoist name Master Black Horn. When you reach Ye Commandery, you may convey Zuo Ci’s regards.” With that, he flicked his sleeves and departed.

p.src: The men transporting the mandarins reached Ye Commandery, presented themselves to Cao Cao, and offered up the fruit. Cao Cao cut one open himself, but it was nothing more than an empty rind with no flesh inside. Greatly startled, Cao Cao questioned the men who had fetched them. They told him what had happened with Zuo Ci. Cao Cao refused to believe them. Suddenly the gatekeeper reported, “A gentleman calling himself Zuo Ci requests an audience with Your Majesty.” Cao Cao summoned him inside. The men who had fetched the mandarins said, “This is the very man we met on the road.” Cao Cao rebuked him: “By what sorcery did you steal away my fine fruit?” Zuo Ci laughed and said, “How could such a thing be?” He took a mandarin and cut it open; it was filled with flesh and tasted exceedingly sweet. Yet every one that Cao Cao cut open himself was an empty rind.

p.src: Cao Cao grew still more astonished and gave Zuo Ci a seat, then questioned him. Zuo Ci asked for wine and meat, and Cao Cao ordered them brought. He drank five dou of wine without becoming drunk and ate a whole sheep without being satisfied. Cao Cao asked, “What arts have enabled you to attain such powers?” Zuo Ci replied, “This poor Daoist studied the Way for thirty years on Mount Emei by the Jialing River in western Sichuan. One day I suddenly heard a voice within a stone wall calling my name; but when I looked, I could see nothing. This continued for several days, until suddenly a thunderbolt shattered the stone wall, revealing three volumes of a celestial book entitled The Heavenly Book of the Arts of Concealment. The upper volume is called Celestial Concealment, the middle volume Earthly Concealment, and the lower volume Human Concealment. Celestial Concealment enables one to mount the clouds, ride the wind, and soar into the great void; Earthly Concealment enables one to pass through mountains and penetrate stone; Human Concealment enables one to roam the four seas, hide or transform one’s shape, and take men’s heads with flying swords and hurled blades. Your Highness has risen to the highest rank a subject may attain. Why not withdraw and follow this poor Daoist to Mount Emei to cultivate the Way? I shall then bestow all three volumes of the celestial book upon you.” Cao Cao said, “I too have long thought of courageously withdrawing at the height of success, but unfortunately the court has not yet found the right man.” Zuo Ci laughed and said, “Liu Xuande of Yizhou is a descendant of the imperial house. Why not yield your position to him? Otherwise, this poor Daoist shall take your head with a flying sword.” Cao Cao flew into a rage. “This fellow is plainly a spy sent by Liu Bei!” He shouted for his attendants to seize him. Zuo Ci only laughed without cease. Cao Cao ordered more than ten jailers to take him away and torture him. The jailers beat him with all their strength, but when they looked at Zuo Ci, he was fast asleep and snoring, wholly untouched by pain. Enraged, Cao Cao ordered a great cangue brought, had it fastened with iron nails and secured with iron chains, then sent Zuo Ci into prison under guard. Yet the cangue and chains all fell away, and Zuo Ci lay on the ground without the least injury. He was kept imprisoned for seven days without food or drink. When they went to look, Zuo Ci was sitting upright on the ground, his complexion rosier than before. The jailers reported this to Cao Cao, who had Zuo Ci brought out and questioned him. Zuo Ci said, “I can go without eating for decades and suffer no harm; and if I eat a thousand sheep in a day, I can finish them all.” Cao Cao was at a complete loss.

p.src: That day, all the officials came to the royal palace for a grand banquet. While the wine was being served, Zuo Ci appeared in wooden clogs and stood before the banquet席. All the officials stared in astonishment. Zuo Ci said, “Your Highness has prepared every delicacy from land and water today and laid a great feast for your ministers, with rare products from every quarter in abundance. Whatever is still lacking, this poor Daoist will fetch for you.” Cao Cao said, “I want dragon liver for a soup. Can you obtain it?” Zuo Ci replied, “What difficulty is there in that?” Taking an ink brush, he painted a dragon on a whitewashed wall and swept his sleeve across it; the dragon’s belly opened of itself. From within the dragon’s belly Zuo Ci drew out a whole dragon liver, still dripping fresh blood. Cao Cao did not believe him and snapped, “You had it hidden in your sleeve beforehand!” Zuo Ci said, “It is now winter, and all the plants and trees are withered; whatever fine flower Your Highness desires, you have only to name it.” Cao Cao said, “I want only peonies.” Zuo Ci said, “That is easy.” He ordered a large flowerpot placed before the banquet and sprayed it with water from his mouth. In moments, a peony plant sprang forth and opened two blossoms. The officials were greatly astonished and invited Zuo Ci to sit and dine with them.

p.src: A short while later, the cook presented sliced raw fish. Zuo Ci said, “For sliced fish to be truly delicious, it must be made from Songjiang perch.” Cao Cao said, “It is a thousand li away. How can you obtain one?” Zuo Ci replied, “That too is no difficult matter!” He had a fishing rod brought and cast his line into the fishpond below the hall. In moments he pulled out several dozen large perch and laid them in the hall. Cao Cao said, “My pond already had such fish in it.” Zuo Ci said, “Why does Your Highness deceive yourself? All other perch under heaven have only two gill covers; only Songjiang perch have four. That is how they may be distinguished.” The officials examined them and found that they did indeed have four gill covers. Zuo Ci said, “To cook Songjiang perch, one must have purple-sprouted ginger.” Cao Cao asked, “Can you obtain that as well?” Zuo Ci replied, “Easily.” He ordered a golden basin brought and covered it with his robe. Presently the basin was filled with purple-sprouted ginger, which he presented before Cao Cao. As Cao Cao reached in to take some, he suddenly found a book inside the basin entitled The New Book of Mengde. Cao Cao picked it up and examined it; not a single character differed from his own work. Cao Cao became deeply suspicious. Zuo Ci took a jade cup from the table, filled it with fine wine, and offered it to Cao Cao, saying, “Your Highness, drink this wine and you shall live a thousand years.” Cao Cao said, “You drink first.”

p.src: Zuo Ci drew the jade hairpin from his cap and traced it through the cup, dividing the wine into two halves; he drank one half himself and offered the other to Cao Cao. Cao Cao rebuked him. Zuo Ci tossed the cup into the air, where it changed into a white dove and flew around the hall. The officials looked up at it, and when they looked back, Zuo Ci had vanished. Suddenly an attendant reported, “Zuo Ci has gone out through the palace gate.” Cao Cao said, “Such a sorcerer must be eliminated! Otherwise, he will surely bring disaster.” He therefore ordered Xu Chu to lead three hundred armored soldiers in pursuit and capture him. Xu Chu mounted his horse and led the troops to the city gate, where he saw Zuo Ci ahead in his wooden clogs, strolling slowly along. Xu Chu galloped after him, yet could not catch up. He chased him all the way into the hills, where a young shepherd came driving a flock of sheep; Zuo Ci slipped into their midst. Xu Chu shot an arrow at him, but Zuo Ci disappeared. Xu Chu slaughtered the entire flock and returned.

p.src: The young shepherd stood guard over the sheep and wept. Suddenly one of the sheep’s heads on the ground spoke in a human voice and called to him, “Put all the sheep’s heads back against the bodies of the dead sheep.” The boy was terrified, covered his face, and fled. Suddenly he heard someone behind him call, “Do not be frightened and run away. I shall restore your sheep to life.” The boy looked back and saw that Zuo Ci had already rejoined the dead sheep and restored them to life, and was driving them toward him. The boy hurried forward to question him, but Zuo Ci had already swept his sleeves and departed; he moved as though flying and vanished in an instant.

p.src: The boy returned and told his master, who dared conceal nothing and reported the matter to Cao Cao. Cao Cao had Zuo Ci’s likeness drawn and circulated, ordering his arrest everywhere. Within three days, throughout the city and beyond, three or four hundred men were arrested who all looked alike: blind in one eye, lame in one leg, wearing white rattan caps, blue Daoist robes, and wooden clogs. The whole marketplace was thrown into an uproar. Cao Cao ordered his commanders to drench them with the blood of pigs and sheep, then escort them to the drill ground south of the city. Cao Cao personally led five hundred armored soldiers to surround them and had every one beheaded. From every severed neck rose a stream of blue vapor. The streams flew into the sky and gathered together, transforming into a single Zuo Ci. He beckoned a white crane from the heavens, mounted it, and clapped his hands in laughter, crying, “When the earth-rat follows the metal-tiger, the treacherous hero’s end shall come in a day!”
